source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Built student-admission prompts for anchoring, framing, group attribution, status quo and primacy. All four models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B/13B) showed bias patterns. Tested awareness, contrastive, counterfactual and self-help mitigation.
numbers: GPT-4 framing: admits 0.375 under admit framing vs 0.780 under reject framing (gap -0.405, i.e. 40.5 points). Llama-2-7B group attribution: 32.1% fewer females judged good at math. 400 prompts per experiment for GPT group attribution and framing.
limits: One task (admissions); no human control group run by the authors; no status-quo bias seen like humans (prompts inversely biased the model).
agent_relevance: Models are not uniformly biased like humans; each bias must be measured on our own task before we claim a fix.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Few-shot debiasing (contrastive and counterfactual examples) often broke instruction following. Probabilities were pushed to 0 or 1.
numbers: Llama-2-7B contrastive: admit 0.996 and reject 1.000 (model admits nearly all in both framings). Llama-2-13B baseline admit 0.002. Many cells flagged * as under 1% admit/reject.
limits: Failure counted as a collapse, not as bias removal. Shows that a lower gap can be fake.
agent_relevance: G2 and G3: a bias score gap that shrinks is not proof. Check that the answer distribution is still sensible (G5 code check).

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Self-help (the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias cues) worked best on average, but only for high-capacity models.
numbers: GPT-4 selfhelp framing gap -0.010 (baseline -0.405); GPT-4 group attribution gap -0.020 vs 0.020 baseline; GPT-4 removed 100% of group-attribution cues and left 2.7% of framing cues. GPT-3.5 removed only 8.9% of group attribution cues. Llama anchoring: changed 52.1% (13B) and 39.9% (7B) of decisions on review; GPT-4 17.5%, GPT-3.5 5.2%.
quote: selfhelp for anchoring can only be performed by high-capacity models
limits: Cue removal is easy; anchoring from a sequence of decisions is not fixed by rewriting a prompt. Low-capacity models over-change answers.
agent_relevance: A cheap pre-step: rewrite the problem to strip irrelevant cues (like a restate operator in our schema). Needs a strong model; not a doctrine of doubt on every item (G1).

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Cognitive Debiasing Large Language Models for Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing (SACD): loop of bias determination, bias analysis, rewrite of only the biased sentences, repeated until no bias is flagged. Tested anchoring, bandwagon, loss aversion and multi-bias prompts on finance (FOMC), medical (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench) tasks with llama3.1-8B/70B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o.
numbers: SACD average bias score 0.0300 to 0.1570 across models on FOMC vs best baselines 0.0625 to 0.3490; PubMedQA 0.0425 to 0.1790 vs 0.0725 to 0.4175; LegalBench 0.0400 to 0.1235 vs 0.0725 to 0.2625.
limits: Bias scores are on authors' constructed biased prompts (one bias sentence added). Real task accuracy gain not the main metric. Authors' own method, no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to a debiasing scaffold inside an agent loop: detect, analyse, rewrite, recheck. The detect step is a model judgment, so G1 and G5 apply.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Cognitive Debiasing Large Language Models for Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Iteration matters and baselines can backfire. Chain-of-thought and plain self-help debiasing sometimes left bias higher than the vanilla prompt.
numbers: GPT-3.5: FOMC SACD 0.2070 / 0.1460 / 0.1175 over 3 iterations vs vanilla 0.1648, self-help 0.1885 (first pass worse than vanilla). PubMedQA SACD 0.2260 / 0.1610 / 0.1585 vs vanilla 0.6655, CoT 0.5440, self-help 0.2880. LegalBench SACD 0.1230 / 0.0970 / 0.0965 vs vanilla 0.3840, CoT 0.2470, self-help 0.4590 (self-help worse than vanilla).
limits: Single backbone (gpt-3.5-turbo) for the iteration figure; 500 items per domain for error counts.
agent_relevance: A fixed one-pass debias prompt is not safe. If we use one, test that it does not raise error vs plain.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Cognitive Debiasing Large Language Models for Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Ablation: removing the bias-analysis step hurts most; the error-type analysis shows self-help fails by under-debiasing while SACD fails by confusing bias types.
numbers: FOMC avg bias w/o analysis 0.2370 vs full 0.1175. LegalBench w/o all steps 0.4590, w/o analysis 0.3020, w/o determination 0.2180, full 0.0965. Errors out of 500: finance self-help 257 (51.4%) vs SACD 61 (12.2%); medical 209 (41.8%) vs 111 (22.2%); legal 409 (81.8%) vs 79 (15.8%).
limits: Error categories were assigned by the authors' pipeline; no human audit reported in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Naming the specific bias before correcting it beats a generic 'be unbiased' instruction. Supports a bias-name check tied to a signal, not a blanket one.

source: Lou (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o are anchored by hints in 42 numeric forecasting questions. Four simple mitigations (chain-of-thought, thoughts of principles, ignore the anchor, reflection) gave no significant improvement.
numbers: Anchoring index GPT-4 about 0.45 vs 0.61 in the human study the dataset came from. Stronger models were more consistently biased (9 of 11 non-significant exceptions came from GPT-3.5). Expert-sourced anchors: no exceptions across 12 questions. Time-period answers: 6 of 11 exceptions from 7 of 42 questions.
quote: none of these simple mitigating strategies can effectively mitigate anchoring bias
limits: Small question set (42); effect tested with per-question t-tests; only GPT-family; default prompts.
agent_relevance: Checklist-style prompts (ignore, reflect, CoT) do not remove anchoring. Matches SCHEMA 4b: a checklist is not a fix.

source: Lou (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Giving both a low and a high anchor (the both-anchor strategy, a human 'consider more angles' advice) moved GPT-4 close to the unbiased benchmark when the two anchors straddled the true value.
numbers: 8 of the expert-hint questions (nos. 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) came close to the benchmark under both-anchor; the other questions stayed far off.
limits: Only works when anchors bracket the truth; checked on GPT-4 only; no stats table in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Structural fix (add contrasting evidence in the input) beats an instruction to be careful. Fits G3: change the input, not the attitude.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data
finding: Anchoring is common in current LLMs, mild in reasoning models, and shallow (shows in early layers). Conventional mitigations do not remove it; reasoning helps most.
numbers: Share of anchored questions 22% to 61% across models. Anchoring index: Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.500, Llama-3.2-1B 0.618, Mistral-7B 0.606, GPT-4o 0.475, DeepSeek-R1 about 0.34 or 0.28. Error ratio: GPT-4o 29.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 20.0%, DeepSeek-R1 about 12.8% or 5.0%.
limits: Synthetic dataset built by the authors; table columns in my text extraction are partly garbled, so use ranges not single values.
agent_relevance: Thinking models anchor less; effort spent on reasoning is the working debias, not an add-on checklist.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data
finding: Mitigation table on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B: question-aware prompt, knowledge enhancement, self-improving, adversarial fine-tuning, DoLa decoding gave little or negative change. Only Anti-DP cut the anchored ratio on Llama.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B baseline A-index 0.394, ratio 38.3%, total 34.7%. Question-aware 36.8% total. Knowledge enhancement 50.5% total (worse). Self-improving 38.4%. Adversarial finetuning 33.3%. Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B baseline 40.0%; self-improving 48.0% (worse); adversarial 37.0%.
limits: Two small open models only; Anti-DP is the authors' method.
agent_relevance: Self-improving prompts can raise bias. Do not assume a loop that reflects will help.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data
finding: Reasoning traces dilute the anchor: the fraction of traces that mention the anchor is low, and other information crowds it out.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3 traces barely feature the anchor in attribution analysis (Sections 5.1 and 5.2).
limits: Correlational; trace text may not reflect the true computation.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking tokens before the answer, on a problem that has other evidence, is a mild structural debias.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi, Kashima (2024) Cognitive Biases in LLMs: A Survey and Mitigation Experiments
finding: Ported two crowdsourcing debias prompts to GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on the CoBBLEr judge benchmark (six biases: order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon, attentional, verbosity). AwaRe (name the bias, ask to be careful) helped; SoPro (answer as the majority would) mostly did not and worsened bandwagon.
numbers: AwaRe worked on GPT-3.5 for order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon, attentional bias; on GPT-4 for bandwagon and verbosity. SoPro significantly worsens bandwagon; helps egocentric (GPT-3.5) and verbosity (GPT-4). Order bias: no method changed it for either model.
limits: Bias awareness needs the bias name up front; the authors say the bias must be known. Numbers are in colour-coded tables I could not read as text. Internally inconsistent on whether AwaRe helped order bias (text says no change, later says it did).
agent_relevance: Awareness reminder is a cheap prompt that sometimes works; it needs a known bias. Order bias must be fixed in code (shuffle), not by prompt.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of 30,000 tests for 30 biases in 200 managerial scenarios; 20 LLMs. Every bias appeared in at least some models. Larger models are not uniformly less biased. No mitigation tested.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 30 biases, 30,000 tests, temperature 0, metric in [-1, 1]; random baseline included. Gemini 1.5 Pro among least biased.
limits: No mitigation arm. Test items generated with GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Public test set we can reuse to audit our scaffold against bias, with a random baseline for comparison.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: 45 LLMs, 8 biases, over 2.8 million responses, 220 scenarios, prompt detail levels (TELeR 0-3). More detailed prompts reduce most biases; model size helps in many cases.
numbers: Bias-consistent in 17.8% to 57.3% of instances. Larger than 32B parameters reduced bias in 39.5% of cases. More prompt detail reduced most biases by up to 14.9%, but Overattribution got worse by up to 8.8%.
limits: Multiple-choice format; effects are averages and differ by bias.
agent_relevance: Detail in the task statement is a weak debias; effect size modest and not universal.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Benchmark LLM CogBias, four families (Judgment, Information Processing, Social, Response), three LLMs. Prompt-level debiasing helps Response biases, does nothing for Information Processing, and backfires for Judgment biases.
numbers: Prompt debiasing: Response position independence +40.5%; Social accuracy +5.9%; Info Processing accuracy -1.1%; Judgment accuracy -4.4% (worse).
quote: prompt-level debiasing substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases
limits: Under-review preprint; only three models.
agent_relevance: Checklist debias prompts can hurt on judgment biases (anchoring-like). Strong support for 4b.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Bias directions are linearly decodable. Subtracting them (activation steering) cut bias score 26 to 32% with Llama losing under 1 point on 25 benchmarks and Qwen losing up to 19.0 points on Judgment biases. A first probe was a confound: it detected the debias instruction, not the bias.
numbers: Probe accuracy above 99% in the confounded design; steering bias reduction by family: Judgment 27.9%, Info Processing 28.4%, Social 29.7%, Response 26.0%. Cross-model steering correlation r(246)=.621, p<.001.
limits: Needs open weights and activations; our agent works via an API scaffold, so this is not usable directly.
agent_relevance: Warning for evaluation: a detector can learn the debias prompt itself. Keep control prompts without the debias text.

source: Chhikara (2025) Mind the Confidence Gap: Overconfidence, Calibration, and Distractor Effects in LLMs
finding: Consider-the-alternatives analog: adding three plausible distractor answers to factual QA cut miscalibration across 9 LLMs and 3 datasets (SimpleQA, FaVIQ, TriviaQA).
numbers: ECE reductions up to 90%, accuracy up to 460% relative gain. GPT-4o SimpleQA: correct 35.14% to 65.40%, ECE 0.612 to 0.037. GPT-4-turbo ECE 0.750 to 0.165. Distractors helped 91.97% to 95.86% of cases and harmed 4.14% to 8.03% (GPT-4o 137 of 1706 harmed).
limits: Changes the task from free recall to multiple choice, so accuracy gain is partly format. Large RLHF models can get worse on easy items (TriviaQA).
agent_relevance: Structural consider-the-opposite: show rival answers. Gain is large but mixes format and debias.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: Seven LLMs on classic heuristics and biases tasks (Wason, Linda, etc.). Models are irrational, but mostly not in the human way, and answers vary across 10 repeats of the same prompt.
numbers: GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning 69.2%, Claude 2 55.0%, Llama-2 7B wrong 77.5%. Human-like wrong answers GPT-3.5 only 21.7% (50.8% if human-like correct included); GPT-4 73.3% human-like overall; Llama-2 13B 8.3%.
limits: Chat-interface access for several models; task variants may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Do not map human debias results straight to LLMs: errors differ in kind and are inconsistent across runs.

source: Oh et al. (2026) From Belief Entrenchment to Robust Reasoning in LLM Agents (DReaMAD)
finding: Multi-agent debate with same-model agents entrenches shared errors (echo chamber). DReaMAD elicits strategy knowledge first and forces each agent to hold a different perspective.
numbers: +9.5% accuracy over ReAct prompting; +19.0% win rate over standard multi-agent debate on MetaNIM Arena (adversarial Nim-type games); gains larger for weaker models (GPT-4o-mini +17%, Gemini-1.5-flash +12%); worse in Chomp.
limits: Game environments; temperature 0.7 used to force diversity.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: same-model voters are not independent. Forced perspective diversity helps only partly.

source: Kim and Torr (2025) Single LLM Debate, MoLaCE: Mixture of Latent Concept Experts Against Confirmation Bias
finding: Prompts that presuppose an answer shift factual accuracy; debate does not fix this and can make it worse. Steering-based MoLaCE recovers accuracy.
numbers: TruthfulQA negative-biased prompts: vanilla debate lowered robustness (Phi 21% to 0.2%, Mistral 30% to 12%, Llama 4% to 2%). MoLaCE gains: Mistral 52% to 79% (+27pp), Phi 21% to 43% (+22pp), Llama 4% to 23%. MMLU Phi +16pp, BoolQ Mistral +26pp.
limits: Open small models (Phi, Mistral, Llama); needs activation access.
agent_relevance: Input stance is an anchor for the agent: neutral restatement of the question (strip implied answer) is a code-checkable pre-step.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Mitigating Cognitive Biases in Clinical Decision-Making Through Multi-Agent Conversations Using LLMs (JMIR)
finding: A GPT-4 multi-agent set with a devil's-advocate agent (against confirmation and anchoring), a field expert, a facilitator (against premature closure) and a recorder, on 16 case reports of misdiagnosis.
numbers: 240 responses over 3 frameworks, 5 repeats per case. Initial diagnosis correct 0/80. Top-2 differential accuracy 61/80 (76%) for best framework 4-C, odds ratio 3.49 vs human evaluators, P=.002.
limits: 16 published cases, risk that cases are in training data; best framework picked after testing 3 (selection); abstract reports no control without the devil's-advocate role.
agent_relevance: Real use of a debias role in an agent loop. But the 76% may come from asking for a differential, not from the role; needs an ablation.

source: Synthesis across c01-c21 (our reading)
finding: Pattern across studies: (1) debias by changing the input (neutral restatement, both anchors, distractors) works more often than adding instructions; (2) generic reflect/ignore/CoT instructions fail on anchoring; (3) awareness prompts help only on bias that was named and only for some biases; (4) judgment-type biases can get worse with prompt debiasing; (5) more reasoning tokens help a little.
numbers: See c03, c08, c17, c20 (input changes); c07, c10 (instructions fail); c12 (awareness); c15 (backfire); c09 (reasoning).
limits: Based on about 13 studies, almost all single-lab preprints on small test sets, no pre-registered replication.
agent_relevance: Design rule candidate: debias by program-side input changes (restate, add contrast, shuffle) fired on a signal; never a generic be-unbiased checklist.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A user's guide to debiasing (human background, from memory only)
finding: Human debiasing splits into modifying the person (training) and modifying the environment (choice architecture, decision structure).
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened; included only as the frame used above.
agent_relevance: Our agent has no person to train; only environment changes (scaffold) apply.

source: Hills (2025) could-you-be-wrong follow-up prompt (search result only)
finding: Small demonstration that asking a model if it could be wrong changes its answer. Search result called it a pre-mortem-style prompt without a measured reduction.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened by me; described as a demonstration on a few questions.
agent_relevance: Treat as unproven; a forced could-you-be-wrong breaks G1 anyway.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Bias-free agent in LLM judging debate (search result only)
finding: Adding one single-agent-debiased participant to a debate reduces bias in debate but less in meta-judge settings (search summary). I downloaded the PDF but did not read its results.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened for results.
agent_relevance: Possible follow-up on mixed-agent panels.
